title: Bright Young Things
full_review:
Actor-writer Stephen Fry ("Wilde," "Gosford Park") makes a mostly successful directorial debut with "Bright Young Things" (ThinkFilm), his own adaptation of Evelyn Waugh's famous novel, "Vile Bodies," an alternately funny and serious look at the upper-crust 1920s' Jazz Age sensation-seekers who partied till they dropped, obsessed with drink and drugs on the road to self-destruction.

Overly fond of long, fast pan shots and annoying quick cutting (much like "Chicago") utilized to show the fast-paced lives these self-absorbed characters lead, the film barely slows down until the end, when the story takes a somber turn.

At the center is writer Adam Symes (Stephen Campbell Moore), whose memoirs are seized by narrow-minded customs agents as he returns to England from Paris. This is particularly unfortunate, as he needs an advance of 1,000 British pounds from publishing magnate Lord Monomark (Dan Aykroyd) to be able to wed his fiancee, Nina (Emily Mortimer).

At his boarding house, he wins an equivalent amount at cards, but then gambles the money on a horse called Indian Runner when a drunken major (Jim Broadbent) assures him the horse is a shoo-in. The major disappears, leading him to think he'll never see the money again. Lo and behold, the horse wins, and throughout the film Adam keeps running into the major, but for complicated reasons never seems to get his hands on the money he's owed.

In desperation, he summons up the courage to ask Nina's loony father (Peter O'Toole) for the money. Surprisingly, the father agrees, but in his carelessness signs the check "Charlie Chaplin," rendering the check worthless.

Since it appears Adam will never get the money, the pragmatic Nina decides to marry the wealthy Ginger (David Tennant), though she still loves Adam.

Adam is eventually hired to be a gossip columnist -- "Mr. Chatterbox" -- after Simon Balcairn (James McAvoy), who had the job, writes an outrageous column filled with libelous fabrications of high-placed people, and then commits suicide. (At one point, Adam fleetingly considers suicide, too.)

For a while, Adam fills his shoes admirably, until an unfortunate mishap.

Eventually war comes, bringing the wanton frivolity of these bright young things to an end.

Fry has seen in Waugh's story a searing indictment of a celebrity culture filled with gossip columnists and paparazzi, long before our present-day obsession with such gossip-generating engines as the National Enquirer and the E! channel.

The film is peopled with various colorful characters, including Adam's kindly, eccentric landlady (a delightful turn by British musical star Julia MacKenzie), who's extraordinarily magnanimous about Adam's rent; a wild sophisticate named Agatha Runcible (Fenella Woolgar) who, in a pivotal scene, wreaks havoc as she tears off into the countryside in a racing car; and an effeminate fop named Miles (Michael Sheen) whose infatuation with another man leads him into serious trouble with the police.

The film is extravagantly cast with some terrific English actors in roles large and small. Besides those mentioned, there are Sir John Mills, Richard E. Grant, Simon Callow, Margaret Tyzack and Jim Carter. Americans Aykroyd and Stockard Channing (as an evangelist traveling with a choir of attractive young ladies) hold their own.

There's much decadent posing and snorting of cocaine and such in the party scenes, but, as in the book -- a classic of social criticism -- it's all for a moral purpose. "Oh, Nina, what a lot of parties," Adam sighs wearily at one point, voicing Waugh's sentiments. The central characters ultimately come to a realization of the more important things of life. Waugh himself was Catholic, and his Catholicism reached its popular apotheosis with the 1982 miniseries, "Brideshead Revisited."

Fry has fiddled a bit with the time frame of the book so that the story now reaches its climax during World War II, and ties things up in a more neatly sentimental fashion than Waugh did. (The novel was published in 1928.) Otherwise, if the story isn't completely faithful in detail, it certainly is in spirit.

The production is handsomely designed (by Michael Howells). The music score encompasses mostly period recordings, everything from "Sing, Sing, Sing" to Noel Coward ditties.

Because of recreational drug and alcohol use, implied promiscuity, generalized decadence, amoral behavior and a suicide, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
